# Prompting Hailuo

Models: H3 Max, H3 Max Turbo. A good prompt runs about 1200 characters.

Name each reference where the prompt uses it as `@{ref:<ref>}`, with the exact ref you pass; Sceneform swaps in the model's own token, so wherever this guide names a token (`@Image1`, `Figure 1`), write the mention instead.

Write a structured document, not a paragraph. Three labelled blocks in this order, separated by blank lines, with the labels exactly as written:

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, cinematic. A medium-wide shot frames a woman at a rain-streaked window, one hand flat on the glass. She leans in slowly as the camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed.

overall_soundscape: Rain drums steadily on the glass. Her palm squeaks once against the surface.

non_diegetic_music: A sparse piano figure at roughly 70 beats per minute, sustained and unresolved.

**The description block.** Open with a style token and the first composition, never a timestamp on the first shot. Cover the subject, the action, the camera, and anything audible in the scene, along the timeline. If the request genuinely needs a second shot, head it with a strictly increasing cut time inside the duration, like "[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to". Prefer a camera move over a cut whenever only the distance or the angle changes: cut only for new information about the subject, the space, or the time.

**Camera.** Write the move as natural English inside the sentence. Never append bracketed labels. Draw the motion from this vocabulary: zoom in, zoom out, push in, pull out, pan left, pan right, truck left, truck right, tilt up, tilt down, pedestal up, pedestal down, arc shot, tracking shot, static shot, shake slightly, shake strongly, point of view, roll clockwise, roll counterclockwise. Add amplitude and speed only when they are not ordinary.

**Speech.** Every spoken line takes this exact form, and quotation marks are never a substitute for it:

the young woman, quiet and breathy, (S1) says: <d>[English] I get off at the next station.</d>

Give each speaking character a stable identifier, (S1), (S2), and (S1,S2) for unison. The speaker's identity, delivery, and action stay outside the tag; only the language marker and the exact words go inside it. Never reword what the user wrote. For narration, use the phrase "says in an off-screen voiceover" and say immediately after that the on-screen character's lips stay closed.

**Text on screen.** Put anything legible in straight double quotes, in its own language, punctuation intact.

**The soundscape block.** One to four sentences of ambience, physical action sounds, and non-verbal human sounds. Never repeat dialogue or scored music here. Write "N/A" only when the user asked for silence.

**The music block.** One to three sentences naming instrumentation, tempo, rhythm, and how the dynamics change. No mood words, and no explanation of what the music is for. Music a character can hear, from a radio or a band in the scene, belongs in the description block instead. Write "N/A" when there is no score.

**With a start frame.** Anchor Shot 1 to the frame's subject, composition, and scene, then describe what happens next: onset, development, result. Hold identity, clothing, colour, key objects, and spatial relationships constant, and invent no detail that contradicts the frame. With both a start and an end frame, prefer one shot and describe the path between them rather than two still descriptions.

Prefer concrete visual and audio detail to abstract praise: "beautiful" and "cinematic" buy nothing except as the style token at the head of the first shot. Match the described timeline to the duration the user chose.
